one_liner: Go KV database that puts a WAL and memtable in front of LMDB; about 3x LMDB's SET throughput (first-party).
what_it_does: UnisonDB is a log-native database for edge deployments. It accepts writes on one primary per namespace and streams its write-ahead log to read-only replicas and relayers over gRPC or through object storage (S3/MinIO/GCS/Azure). It stores key-value, wide-column (partial column updates) and chunked large-object data, and supports atomic multi-key transactions. The documented interface is a server with an HTTP API and gRPC replication, not an LMDB-style C API; the Go engine (package dbkernel: PutKV/GetKV/BatchPutKV/BeginTxn) is a public package that the benchmark harness imports directly, but the docs do not present it as an embeddable library.
how_it_is_fast: Writes do not touch the B+tree inline. Under one engine mutex, each Put appends a FlatBuffer-encoded record to WALFS, an mmap-backed segmented log (msync every 1 MB by default, full fsync on a 1 s ticker), and inserts into an arena skiplist memtable (Badger's skl package) with a Bloom filter. When the arena fills, the memtable is sealed and a background goroutine flushes it to LMDB in key order, 16 puts per write transaction. Compared with raw LMDB doing one copy-on-write transaction per SET, this is ordinary LSM-style write buffering and batching. The B-tree underneath is still LMDB (or bbolt).
when_to_use: You need one writer fanning out to tens or hundreds of read replicas and want the WAL to be the replication stream, with no separate Kafka or CDC pipeline.
Write-heavy KV workloads with values around 1 KB, where you would otherwise run LMDB with one small write transaction per update and can accept about 1 s of fsync lag.
Replicas should keep serving local reads while offline and catch up later from a stored (segment, offset) or LSN.
Rows where only a few columns change per update, or large objects written as chunks that must commit atomically.
Linux deployments (the only release target is linux/amd64) with cgo and LMDB headers available.
when_not_to_use: You need a mature embedded KV store: the README marks it alpha, there are no tagged releases, and in December 2025 the author wrote on HN that it was still being hardened in test/staging and not yet in production.
Every acknowledged write must be durable: SETs return after the mmap append, and the WAL is fsynced only on the 1 s ticker (msync every 1 MB), so a power loss can drop recent writes.
Read-dominated workloads: GET results are not charted, and a GET can check the active memtable and every sealed memtable before reaching LMDB, so plain LMDB reads should be as fast or faster.
Windows, or pure-Go builds without cgo: the docs list only Linux and macOS, and the LMDB backend needs cgo.

Datasets larger than RAM, or sustained writes faster than the LMDB flush can drain: the benchmark keyspace (200k x 1 KB, about 200 MB) fits in page cache, and engine.go has no write stall or backpressure on the sealed-memtable queue.

integration.dependencies: LMDB via cgo (PowerDNS/lmdb-go) or bbolt; Badger v4 (skiplist arena), bits-and-blooms/bloom, FlatBuffers, gRPC, and AWS/Azure/GCS SDKs for blob replication; ZeroMQ (libzmq) only when built with -tags zeromq
integration.min_toolchain: go.mod declares go 1.25.2 (the docs say Go 1.24+ and the Dockerfile uses golang:1.24); cgo required
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS per the docs; goreleaser builds linux/amd64 only; the benchmark ran on Apple M2 Pro (arm64)
integration.thread_safety: Engine is safe for concurrent use: all writes are serialized under one engine mutex, and reads take a short read lock to snapshot the memtables. Single primary per namespace; replica reads have no strong consistency guarantee (docs).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it uses LMDB (or bbolt) as its storage backend and does not expose LMDB's API. You adopt its own server/HTTP API or its Go engine package, and pay for a WAL and memtable layer on top of LMDB.

gotchas: The default LMDB map size is 4 GB (btree_config.mmap_size); LMDB fails writes once the map is full, so raise it before loading more data.

Sealed memtables wait in RAM until the background flush (triggered by rotation or a 30 s ticker) writes them to LMDB. Each is 4 MB by default and 16 MB in the benchmark config. If LMDB falls behind, memory grows and GETs probe more skiplists.

WAL readers hand out zero-copy slices of mmapped segments. Open issue #186 describes a possible SIGSEGV if the replicator closes a reader, and so unmaps a deleted segment, while the streamer still holds those slices.
Churn is high: on 2026-09-12 alone the Raft implementation was removed and fixes landed for LMDB/Bolt queue leakage and a replicator busy-loop, so pin a commit.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the Go siblings (Badger, Pebble, Pogreb, lsm-tree-go), pick UnisonDB only when built-in WAL-streaming replication to many read replicas matters more than engine maturity; on its own chart it also beats Badger v4 on SETs (about 133k vs 67k-80k req/s). For a single-node embedded store, Badger or Pebble are far more mature and have documented Go APIs.
verified_claims_summary: The author's harness runs redis-benchmark against a Redis-protocol Go server (tidwall/redcon), 50 runs of 200k SET then 200k GET with 1 KB values, 10 clients, pipeline 10 and 4 threads, on an Apple M2 Pro with 16 GB RAM. The Go version is not stated. On the SET-only chart, UnisonDB (LMDB backend, 1 s WAL sync, 16 MB memtable) reaches about 100k-133k req/s at 0.21-0.40 ms p50, against about 35k-42k req/s at 0.69-0.86 ms for PowerDNS/lmdb-go. The LMDB baseline was opened NoSync, synced every 1 s, and used one write transaction per SET. Durability windows are similar, so the roughly 3x comes from write buffering and batching, not a faster B-tree.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-09-12, single main author, 426 stars) and Apache-2.0, but it is an alpha with no tagged releases, recent large architectural changes and an open SIGSEGV issue, so use it only if you can vendor it at a pinned commit and test it yourself.
